apollo.name: Apollo 11 · Eagle
apollo.title: Eagle: two parts, different endings
apollo.condition: The lower landing stage is inactive on the Moon. The separate laser reflector still returns light sent from Earth.
apollo.reason: The lower stage was the launch platform for the crew cabin. The cabin lifted off; the landing gear and surface experiments stayed behind.
apollo.ending: The upper cabin was left in lunar orbit after the crew transferred. NSSDCA says its fate is unknown and a later impact is assumed, not confirmed. NASA's artifact catalog does not identify an impact location.
apollo.imageNote: LRO/LROC orbital photograph. NASA page published 19 June 2019; this is not a live image.
apollo.question: Which part is visible in this photograph?
apollo.answer: Eagle's lower landing stage. The upper cabin had already left the surface.

viking.name: Viking 1 · Lander
viking.title: A science station that went quiet
viking.condition: The lander is inactive at its landing site. It no longer sends messages to Earth.
viking.reason: Viking was a stationary science station, not a return spacecraft. It remained where it landed when communication ended.
viking.ending: In November 1982, a faulty command sent from Earth interrupted communications. Attempts to regain contact were unsuccessful.
viking.imageNote: NASA-provided HiRISE lander cutout, PIA01881. Published 5 December 2006; this is not a live image.
viking.question: Did Viking drive away after its mission?
viking.answer: No. It was a lander, not a rover. HiRISE located it at its landing site.

sojourner.name: Sojourner & Pathfinder
sojourner.title: A little rover and a missing relay
sojourner.place: Pathfinder landing region, Ares Vallis, Mars
sojourner.condition: Both are silent. Sojourner needed the Pathfinder lander to relay its messages to Earth; the rover's final parking spot is uncertain.
sojourner.reason: They were sent to study Mars, with no return journey. Once the lander stopped relaying data, the team could no longer talk to the rover.
sojourner.ending: Pathfinder's final data arrived on 27 September 1997. Sojourner was programmed to approach and circle an unresponsive lander, but its actual final movements are not known.
sojourner.imageNote: NASA's annotated HiRISE hardware view, PIA09105, acquired 21 December 2006. MPF marks the Pathfinder lander, not a confirmed Sojourner position.
sojourner.question: Does the orbital image prove exactly where Sojourner stopped?
sojourner.answer: No. The lander is identified; the proposed tiny rover candidate remains uncertain. A likely explanation is not the same as a confirmed observation.
